segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. They bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You say so.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the chief priests kept accusing him of many things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate questioned him again:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have you no answer at all? See how many things they accuse you of.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now at the festival he used to release for them one prisoner, whichever one they asked for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man called Barabbas was in prison with the insurgents who had committed murder in the insurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowd came up and began to ask him to do what he usually did for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you want me to release for you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he realized that the chief priests had handed him over out of envy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate spoke to them again:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Then what do you want me to do with the man you call the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They shouted back,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why? What wrong has he done?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they shouted all the more,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them. He had Jesus flogged and handed him over to be crucified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the governor’s headquarters, and called together the whole cohort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They dressed him in purple, and after weaving a crown of thorns they put it on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they began to salute him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hail, king of the Jews!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They kept striking him on the head with a reed and spitting on him, and falling on their knees they bowed down before him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and dressed him in his own clothes. Then they led him out to crucify him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They pressed into service a passer-by who was coming in from the country, a certain Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought him to the place Golgotha, which translated means Place of a Skull.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They tried to give him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they crucified him and divided his clothes among themselves, casting lots for them to decide who should take what.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was the third hour when they crucified him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The inscription stating the charge against him read: “The King of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With him they crucified two bandits, one on his right and one on his left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who passed by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Ha! You who would destroy the temple and build it in three days,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: save yourself by coming down from the cross!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the chief priests too, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He saved others; himself he cannot save!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Let the Messiah, the king of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even those who were crucified with him taunted him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which translated means,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of those standing by heard it and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, he is calling Elijah!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed his last.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion who stood facing him saw that he breathed his last in this way, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Truly this man was God’s Son!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were also women watching from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who used to follow him and serve him when he was in Galilee, and many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening had already come, since it was Preparation day, that is, the day before the Sabbath,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph of Arimathea came, a respected council member who was himself also waiting for the kingdom of God. He took courage, went in to Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate was amazed that he was already dead, and summoning the centurion he asked him whether he had been dead for long.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he learned from the centurion that it was so, he granted the corpse to Joseph.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the cloth, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was laid.

notes.traditional: Thou sayest it / You have said so
notes.note: The Greek is two words, literally “You say.” It can be read as a qualified yes (“It is as you say”), as a non-committal reply that throws the claim back on the questioner (“Those are your words”), or even as a question. Most scholars take it as deliberately reserved; Pilate’s continued questioning suggests he did not hear a plain confession.

Mark uses the Latin word praetorium, the official residence of a Roman governor. In Jerusalem this was probably either Herod’s former palace or the Antonia fortress beside the temple; which one is disputed. A cohort was nominally several hundred soldiers, though “the whole cohort” may simply mean all who were on duty.

notes.phrase: the father of Alexander and Rufus
notes.note: The two sons play no part in the story, and only Mark names them. The natural explanation is that they were known to Mark’s first readers. A Rufus is greeted in Romans 16:13, but whether he is the same person is uncertain.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning, the sixth (v. 33) about noon, and the ninth (vv. 33–34) about three in the afternoon. John 19:14 gives a different time for the proceedings, a difficulty for which several explanations have been offered and none is agreed.

The Greek word means someone who takes by violence, a brigand or armed raider, not a sneak thief, for which Greek has a different word. Josephus uses it of insurgent bands in Judea, and some translations therefore render it “rebels” here; that sense is possible, especially after v. 7, but is not certain. “Bandits” keeps the element of violence without deciding the question.

notes.phrase: one on his right and one on his left
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add a verse 28: “And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was counted among the lawless.’” It is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably borrowed from Luke 22:37. The edition translated here omits it, which is why the numbering passes from 27 to 29.

The Greek christos means “anointed one” and here is a title, set alongside “the king of Israel” in the priests’ taunt. “Messiah” conveys the title, whereas “Christ” now sounds to most readers like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice, using “Messiah” in the Gospels where the title is the point and “Christ” elsewhere.

The Greek word can mean a particular land or region, or the earth as a whole. Mark may mean darkness over Judea or over the whole world; the text does not decide. Some translations have “the whole earth.”

These are the opening words of Psalm 22 in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus and his followers, which Mark writes out in Greek letters and then translates. The same psalm lies behind earlier details of the scene: the dividing of clothes by lot (v. 24) and the mockers shaking their heads (v. 29). In v. 35 the bystanders take the words as a call to Elijah, who was expected to come to the aid of the righteous in distress.

The temple had two great curtains: one at the entrance to the sanctuary building and one inside it, screening off the Most Holy Place. Mark does not say which is meant; most interpreters think the inner one, but this is disputed. The verb “torn” is the one Mark used of the heavens at Jesus’s baptism (1:10).

The Greek has no article and can be translated “the Son of God” or “a son of God.” On the lips of a Roman soldier the phrase could mean something like a divine or godlike man, and some translations render it that way. Mark, however, plainly means his readers to hear the confession that opens his book (1:1). “God’s Son” leaves both possibilities open, as the Greek does.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a member of a city council. It is usually understood here to mean a member of the Jerusalem council that condemned Jesus, though Mark uses a different word for that body in v. 1 and does not say so explicitly. The adjective translated “respected” can also imply wealth and social standing.

candidates.reason: “Kingdom of God” recurs throughout the Gospels and letters, and translators differ between “kingdom,” “reign” and “rule”; readers need one consistent choice.
“Scribes” suggests copyists to modern readers, and translations vary between “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “legal experts” across the Gospels and Acts.
It names the sanctuary building as distinct from the whole temple complex (ἱερόν); whether to mark that distinction in English (“sanctuary” vs “temple”) should be settled once.
Renderings vary between “thief,” “robber,” “bandit” and “rebel” across the Gospels (e.g. the “den of robbers,” Barabbas in John, the arrest scene), and the choice affects how the crucifixion is read.

The word covers physical prostration, homage to a superior and worship of a deity; a consistent policy on when to use “worship” as against “bow down” or “pay homage” is needed across the Gospels and Revelation.
